# SAIRNfreedom — the four research items from §9a.7–10, answered

**Researched 2026-08-30 from primary sources.** These four were generated by
folding the five detail items into the build spec: each feature name, once
detailed, surfaced an edge the name had hidden. All four are now answered well
enough to build against, and every one of them **changed the design**.

**Not legal, tax or liquor-licensing advice.** Primary-source reads by
non-lawyers, to the same standard as the ORC 2915 and 38 U.S.C. 5901 passes.
Each section carries its own unverified list.

---

# 1. IRS quid-pro-quo — donor pins and the auto-emailed receipt

## The threshold issue nobody asked about, and it outranks the pin

**§ 170(c) puts our five organizations in two different categories with
different conditions**, and the receipt engine has to know which:

- **VFW / American Legion** — § 170(c)(3), *"A post or organization of war
  veterans… no part of the net earnings of which inures to the benefit of any
  private shareholder or individual."* No use-condition.
- **Elks / Moose / Eagles** — § 170(c)(4), domestic fraternal societies under
  the lodge system, deductible *"In the case of a contribution or gift by an
  individual… **but only if such contribution or gift is to be used exclusively
  for religious, charitable, scientific, literary, or educational purposes**"*
  or prevention of cruelty to children or animals.

**So an unconditional "your gift is tax-deductible" receipt is a claim the
statute does not support for a fraternal lodge's general-fund or social gifts,
and is limited to individuals.** Deductibility is a **gate before the receipt
renders**, configured per org type and per designated use — not a fixed string.

**This is the third independent legal regime that splits on the
veterans/fraternal axis**, after ORC 2915.01 (V)(2)/(V)(3) and the officer-title
vocabulary. Federal tax law, Ohio gaming law, and internal governance all fork
at the same place. That is the product's central design axis, not a coincidence.

## The operative rules

**IRC § 6115** — disclosure required on a quid pro quo contribution **in excess
of $75** (exactly $75 does not trigger). The statement must (1) inform the donor
the deductible amount is limited to the excess of the payment over the value of
goods or services, and (2) give a **good faith estimate** of that value. The $75
tests **the payment**, not the deductible portion.

**IRC § 170(f)(8)** — contemporaneous written acknowledgment at **$250 or more,
per contribution**, containing the amount, whether goods or services were
provided, and a description and good faith estimate of their value.
**26 CFR 1.170A-13(f)(1) expressly forbids aggregating** to reach $250:
*"Separate contributions of less than $250 are not subject to the requirements
of section 170(f)(8), regardless of whether the sum… equals $250 or more."*

**§ 6714 penalty** — $10 per contribution, capped at $5,000 per fundraising
event or mailing. **Not inflation-adjusted.**

## The safe harbor figures, and a trap in the IRS's own publication

**Current (TY2026), from Rev. Proc. 2025-32 § 4.33:**

| Base guideline | **2026** | 2025 | Governs |
|---|---|---|---|
| $5 | **$13.90** | $13.60 | Low-cost-article **cost** ceiling (the org's cost) |
| $25 | **$69.50** | $68.00 | Minimum **payment** for the logo route |
| $50 | **$139** | $136.00 | Cap in the "lesser of 2% or $X" **FMV** test |

**PUBLICATION 1771 IS THREE YEARS STALE.** It is Rev. 11-2023 and prints
**$125 / $62.50 / $12.50**, with its own footnote admitting *"The dollar amounts
are for 2023."* The IRS's plain-English publication is the obvious place a
developer would look, and building from it hardcodes wrong numbers. **Figures
must load per tax year from the annual Revenue Procedure.**

**§ 513(h)(2)(B) aggregates the items, per donor, per calendar year:** *"If more
than 1 item is distributed… to a single distributee in any calendar year, the
aggregate… shall be treated as 1 article."* A pin plus a mug plus a certificate
in one year are tested against $13.90 **combined**.

## The implementable rule

`P` = payment. `FMV` = pin's fair market value. `COST` = lodge's cost of **all**
items to that donor in the same calendar year.

0. **Gate on deductibility.** § 170(c)(4) lodge → only assert deductibility for
   an individual's gift designated to a qualifying purpose. Otherwise the
   receipt must not claim it.
1. **Load the year's figures.** Never hardcode.
2. **Can the pin be disregarded?** Either route, **and** the receipt states the
   deductible amount (the Rev. Proc. 90-12 fund-raising-campaign precondition):
   - **Route A (logo):** `P >= MIN_PAYMENT` **and** the pin bears the lodge name
     or logo **and** `COST <= LOW_COST`
   - **Route B (2%):** `FMV <= min(0.02 * P, FMV_CAP)`
3. **Emit.** Disregarded → omit the value, state no goods or services provided,
   no § 6115 disclosure needed even above $75. Not disregarded and `P > 75` →
   § 6115 disclosure **mandatory**, and Pub 1771 warns *"a disclosure in small
   print within a larger document might not meet this requirement."* Not
   disregarded and `P >= 250` → additionally satisfy § 170(f)(8)(B).

**At the $100 tier:** $100 ≥ $69.50, so a **lodge-emblem** pin costing ≤ $13.90
clears Route A — value omitted, no disclosure. **If the pin carries no lodge
name or logo, Route A is unavailable** and Route B applies: 2% of $100 = **$2.00**.
Almost any pin fails that. **A sharp cliff, and the most likely place the system
silently emits a defective receipt.**

**Membership-benefit exception (26 CFR 1.170A-13(f)(8)(i)(B))** disregards annual
membership benefits at **$75 or less per year** — free/discounted admission,
parking, preferred access, discounts. It covers **recurring privileges, not
physical items**; Pub 1771's own example values a $20 poster separately inside a
$75 membership. **A pin does not ride along on dues.**

## Unverified

- **Whether a premium earned by crossing a *cumulative lifetime* threshold
  attaches to the crossing payment.** No authority found; § 170(f)(8) and § 6115
  are both written per-payment and the only cumulation rule (§ 513(h)(2)(B))
  counts *items*, not contributions. **Genuine gap → tax professional.** Keeping
  the pin inside Route A sidesteps it entirely.
- Rev. Proc. 90-12 § 3 verbatim (predates the IRS online archive; reconstructed
  from three citing sources that agree). Rev. Proc. 92-102. Post-Oct-2025
  guidance. State charitable-solicitation receipt requirements.

# 2. Minor-participant data — COPPA does not apply, ORC 2741 does

## Verdict: COPPA NO, on three independent grounds

For an internal system where an **adult volunteer** keys a child's details from
a **parent-signed paper form** into a **staff-facing** app for a **501(c)**
lodge:

1. **No collection *from a child*.** 16 CFR 312.2 defines collection as
   requesting/prompting/encouraging **a child** to submit online, enabling **a
   child** to make information public, or passive tracking of **a child**. Adult
   data entry is none of these. **This ground alone is sufficient and survives
   even if the lodge were commercial.**
2. **Not collected online.** *"Collected online"* is in the statute
   (15 U.S.C. § 6501(8)), and the FTC's position is that COPPA *"does not apply
   to information submitted to an operator offline"* and covers *"only
   information submitted online, and not information requested online but
   submitted offline."*
3. **Not a covered operator, not directed to children.** Both statute and rule
   limit these to **commercial** actors and exclude nonprofits outside FTC Act
   § 5. FTC: *"COPPA expressly states that the law applies to commercial
   websites and online services and not to nonprofit entities…"*

## It flips to YES if any of these are ever built

- **A child under 13 enters their own information online** — self-registration,
  kids' portal, a score lookup that asks the child for identifying details, a
  photo upload. **Biggest risk, easiest to add by accident.**
- A public or child-visible surface where a child can post or make information
  public.
- The service becomes plausibly *"directed to children"* in look and content.
- The **vendor** markets a commercial child-facing product on the same
  infrastructure — the nonprofit shield belongs to the lodge and does not
  travel.

**Treat "does a child ever type into this system" as an architectural invariant
with an owner, not a product decision a later sprint can quietly reverse.**

## The real Ohio exposure: ORC 2741, and the fundraising prong

**ORC 2741.01 "commercial purpose"** includes, at subdivision **(4)**,
*"For the purpose of fundraising."* There is **no nonprofit exception and no
fraternal-newsletter exception** in Chapter 2741.

Working in the lodge's favour: "persona" requires the aspects to have
**commercial value**; contest-results reporting fits the **newsworthy**
(2741.09(A)(1)(b)) and **event of public concern** (A)(3) exceptions; unnamed
group shots fit (A)(4).

**Working against it:** the *same photo* of a named child is lawful in a
results story and prohibited in a *"help us fund next year's contest"* appeal.
Remedies: statutory damages **$2,500–$10,000** plus possible punitive
(ORC 2741.07).

**And the standard release does not cover it.** The actual 2025-26 Elks Hoop
Shoot registration form bundles the likeness grant into registration — no
separate photo release — scoped to:

> "any and all purposes reasonably related to the conduct and promotion of the
> Elks Hoop Shoot contests"

Granted to **BPOE and the Elks National Foundation, not to a software vendor.**
It does **not** authorise general lodge fundraising or membership recruitment.

**ORC 2741.05 is silent on minors.** A minor owns 100% of their own right of
publicity and cannot contract. Universal practice is the parent's signature —
that is practice filling a statutory silence, not the statute speaking.

## Build rules

**Scoped consent, never a boolean.** Store per participant per consent event:
`consent_scope` as an **enum** — `program_conduct_and_promotion` (the only scope
the Elks form grants), `lodge_newsletter`, `lodge_website`, `social_media`,
`fundraising_or_donation_appeal` — all defaulting false;
`name_may_be_published` **separate from image**; consenting party, relationship,
signature method (ORC 2741.01 accepts *"electronic, digital, or any other
verifiable means"*), timestamp, form version, and an **immutable copy of the
exact consent text shown**; and `revoked_at`.

**Gate publication on scope.** Any workflow tagging an image for fundraising or
recruitment **hard-blocks** unless that scope is granted. That is the concrete
answer to 2741.01(B)(4). Record which consent authorised each published photo,
so revocation can find the images rather than guess.

**Access, default-deny, three roles:** program director (own program and lodge
only, row-level); lodge officer (roster-level, **not** allergies/medical or
parent contact without explicit grant); vendor support (**no standing read**,
break-glass only, time-boxed, audit row per access). Every read of a minor
record audit-logged with actor, record, timestamp and reason code.

**Copy the American Legion's background-check pattern verbatim:** store the
**binary accept / reject only**, never offence detail, never the report — their
2024 Risk Management Guidebook designed it that way explicitly so that *"this
system of reporting eliminates the need to disclose specific criminal history
details."*

**Retention — split the record**, because two pressures point opposite ways.
No legal mandate exists (312.10 binds only COPPA operators; Ohio has none), but
**ORC 2305.111** lets a childhood-abuse claimant sue until roughly **age 30** —
~22 years for an 8-year-old contestant.

- **Thin participation record** (name, program, year, lodge, age group, result,
  supervising adults) — retain long.
- **Fat contact record** (parent phone/email, address, allergies, school,
  shirt size) — purge on a short cycle, default one program year plus one.
- **Photographs** — only while a live consent scope authorises the use.

**Do not build:** child-facing registration, child login or profile, a public
participant directory, an SSN field, **any biometric or face-matching**,
direct staff-to-minor messaging (Legion rule: parent and a second representative
copied, no one-to-one texts, 8 a.m.–8 p.m., per-parent opt-out), behavioural
analytics or third-party trackers on any page rendering a minor's record, and
**school-roster ingestion** — taking data from a school engages FERPA's *"party
acting for the agency"* question (34 CFR 99.31(a)(1)(i)(B)) and ORC 3319.321's
redisclosure condition. **Get everything from the parent and both problems
vanish.**

## Unverified

Post-June-2025 text of 16 CFR 312.2 (eCFR and federalregister.gov both blocked;
quoted from GovInfo's 2023 annual edition — **the statutory basis is unchanged**,
which is why the conclusion holds). COPPA penalty for 2026 ($53,088 confirmed for
2025). FTC's Feb 2026 age-verification policy statement. **Elks Grand Lodge Youth
Protection Guidelines (Code 512200) — existence confirmed, content not public;
whether Elks require background checks for Hoop Shoot volunteers is unknown.**
Moose, VFW and Eagles youth-protection policies — not found. Ohio biometric
statute — none found, not exhaustively searched. Ohio mandatory-reporter status
of lodge volunteers — **not relied on; misreading it permissively is the
dangerous error.**

# 3. Ohio alcohol — the vendor-search feature does not survive, and the replacement is better

## Spirits: one seller, one price, set by the state

**ORC 4301.10(A)(3)** — the Division shall *"establish and maintain a state
monopoly of the distribution of spirituous liquor."* **(B)(4)** — retail prices
*"shall be the same at all state liquor stores."*

**OAC 4301-3-01(A):** *"No permit holder authorized to sell spirituous liquor
within the state shall either directly or indirectly… purchase spirituous liquor
for resale from other than a state liquor store or state liquor agency at
wholesale, except pursuant to express written consent of the division."*

Price is a formula in (D)(1), not a negotiation. **There is nothing to shop.**

## Beer and wine: the prohibition is on the RETAILER, and it hides in a rule about signs

The franchise act (ORC 1333.82–83) binds **manufacturer to distributor** only —
which would wrongly suggest retailers may shop freely. The retailer-side
prohibition is in the Administrative Code, in a rule titled about signs and
fixtures:

**OAC 4301:1-1-43(J)(2):** *"No retail permit holder shall purchase any brand of
alcoholic beverages from any wholesale permit holder, for resale at retail, if
the retail permit premises are located outside the wholesale permit holder's
exclusive sales area or territory, except as provided for in this rule."*

**Per brand, the lodge has exactly one lawful vendor.** Retailers also cannot buy
from each other (OAC 4301:1-1-46(B)).

**Discounts and rebates are banned both directions** — OAC 4301:1-1-43(A)(2):
*"No retail or wholesale permit holder shall accept any premiums, gifts,
discounts based on quantity of sales or any other reason, cash discount sales,
rebates, or kickbacks."* **(K):** *"Depletion allowance programs are
prohibited."* ORC 4301.24(D): beer and US-made wine sold to a retailer **"except
for cash"** — no terms to negotiate.

**Wine additionally has a floor and a posted schedule** — OAC 4301:1-1-03(C):
minimum wholesale markup of **33⅓%**, and a quarterly price schedule stating
*"the container and case price to all wholesale and retail permit holders."*

**Beer** has a minimum **retail** markup of 25% (OAC 4301:1-1-72(B)(3)) for
off-premises sales only; no wholesale floor or posted schedule found.

## The exposure is on the customer's permit

**ORC 4301.58(D)** bars possessing for sale any intoxicating liquor not
purchased from the Division or a permit holder. **ORC 4301.99(C)** makes that a
**first-degree misdemeanor**. **ORC 4301.25(A)** lets the Commission suspend or
revoke a permit for violating *"any lawful rule of the commission"* — the hook
that reaches the territory rule.

**Precision point:** 4301.58(D)'s mandatory-revocation sentence cross-references
division **(C)**, not (D). Do not represent revocation as automatic.

## Build verdict

| Category | Search for better pricing? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Spirits** | **No — meaningless, and a "shop around" flow risks inducing an offense** | State monopoly, uniform statewide price |
| **Beer** | **Largely meaningless per brand**; lawful only as brand-vs-brand cost comparison | One distributor per brand per territory; discounts banned; cash only |
| **Wine** | **No** | Territory bar **plus** 33⅓% floor **plus** posted schedule "to all… permit holders" |
| **Food, gaming supplies, entertainment** | **Yes** | Nothing in Ch. 4301/4303 restricts these. **Caveat:** gaming supplies are separately constrained by ORC 2915 — equipment must come from licensed sources |

**The reframe, and it is a better product than what it replaces:** not "find a
cheaper supplier" but **brand-level cost-per-serving comparison, pour-cost and
waste analysis, menu pricing against the minimum-markup floors, and verifying
the lodge is actually being charged the posted wine schedule price and the state
spirits price.** That last one is a real audit function no verified competitor
performs, and it cannot get anyone's permit pulled.

## Two spec corrections

- **D-4 is the club permit** (ORC 4303.17(A)(1)), and (A)(2) waives the
  three-year existence requirement for *"units of organizations chartered by
  congress"* and subsidiary units of national fraternal organizations.
  **(B) expressly preserves D-4 alcohol service in a room used for bingo.**
- **D-4a is an AIRLINE permit** — ORC 4303.171, for a club sponsored by an
  airline company at a publicly owned airport. **Never label a lodge permit
  "D4A."**

**Licensing crossover:** ORC 4303.17(A)(1) conditions D-4 issuance **and
retention** on all elected officers certifying the club is maintained by a
dues-paying membership, with the roster available on request. **The membership
module is therefore already touching a liquor-permit retention condition** —
which belongs in the wholly-unexamined licensing gap (§9a.3).

## Unverified

`com.ohio.gov` Division of Liquor Control pages returned **404**; nothing from
the Department of Commerce is relied on. Definition of "alcoholic beverages" in
OAC 4301:1-1-43 (inferred from context). Whether (J)(2) admits any retailer-side
exception. Whether the wine minimum-price rule reaches sealed-container sales to
an on-premises club. Direct-from-producer channels (A-1/A-2/A-3a self-
distribution, S permits) — **could open a narrow real shopping lane for
beer/wine.** Which permits a given lodge actually holds.

# 4. Per-capita and dues waivers — hypothesis half confirmed, half refuted

## Half 1: CONFIRMED — per capita accrues on the roster, regardless of dues status

| Org | Verdict | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| **Elks** | **CONFIRMED** | Per capita is defined **outside** "dues" by Grand-Lodge-mandated by-law text: *"all Members, including Life Members, shall pay the Grand Lodge per capita fee… **in addition to** the appropriate regular or Life Member dues"*, and regular dues *"shall not include"* it. Billed on the **April 1 membership report headcount**, due **May 1** |
| **VFW** | **CONFIRMED** | Sec. 606: national dues *"for every member (except Life Members) of a Post in good standing"* |
| **American Legion** | **CONFIRMED** | Model Post Constitution: the post pays National and Departmental dues *"for every member of the post"* |
| **Moose** | **CONFIRMED, vacuously** | No waiver mechanism exists to test — only Moosehaven residents are exempt (Sec. 30.2) |
| **Eagles** | **UNVERIFIED** | Grand Aerie Constitution is **sold as a physical product**, not published |

## Half 2: REFUTED — "the lodge absorbs it" is one of FOUR patterns

**This is where the working hypothesis was wrong, and it changes the schema.**

1. **The member still pays it personally — Elks.** Waiving lodge dues does not
   touch the per-capita line on the same bill. **Life members pay it too:**
   *"Before issuing annual cards to Life and Honorary Life Members, those Members
   are required by Statute to pay the Grand Lodge per capita dues and
   assessments."* Verified live: San Jose Elks 2026-27 shows **$38.00** Grand
   Lodge per capita for both Life and Regular members.
2. **A designated restricted fund pays it — VFW.** National By-Laws **Sec.
   219(g)** authorises *"Remission of dues of sick, needy or disabled members"*
   as a **Post Relief Fund** expenditure. The fund is ring-fenced: *"shall not be
   loaned to the Post… or transferred from the relief fund in any manner or
   under any guise."* The member stays in good standing and the national portion
   flows normally.
3. **An actuarial endowment pays it — VFW life members.** Sec. 111(d): an amount
   set *"after consultation with professionals licensed in actuarial science"*
   is paid annually *"to Posts, Departments and National Headquarters on all life
   members"*, floors $10.50 / $16.50 / $27.00, with an explicit reduced-payout
   clause if the plan is underfunded.
4. **The lodge genuinely absorbs it — American Legion**, closest to the original
   hypothesis, and only because the Legion has **no national waiver provision at
   all**.

**Schema consequence: `payer` is a separate dimension from the liability.**
Model per-capita as accruing **per member on the roster regardless of dues
status** — that half was right — but the payer is an enum:
`member` | `restricted_fund` | `endowment` | `lodge_general`. **Elks and VFW are
both modelled wrong by a single "lodge absorbs it" assumption.**

## Moose is architecturally inverted, and validates the liability model in its own words

Per capita is **inside** member dues (Sec. 30.2), and the money flows
**member → Moose International → lodge**: *"Dues paid by a member shall be
credited as of the date the dues are posted by Moose International"*, with the
lodge's share deposited back weekly. **The lodge never holds it and cannot
absorb it.**

And the Administrator's Manual states the accounting treatment outright:

> "Dues Moose International Portion entered in **Acct 2515 as liability** ABCD
> per Capita. Dues Lodge Portion entered in Acct 4005 as income."

**Liability versus income, named as such, by the organization's own chart of
accounts.** That is independent confirmation of §2a's pass-through design.

## A misreading to avoid

**The American Legion's military provision waives the FORFEITURE TIMETABLE, not
the dues:** *"may waive the provisions hereof, **upon payment of dues for the
year in which reinstatement occurs**, with reference to former members who have
been prevented from the payment of dues by reason of active military service."*
Easy to read as a dues waiver. It is not.

## Consequences for non-remittance are severe and specific

- **Moose (Sec. 43.6):** the lodge must within **ten days** notify **every
  member** in writing that it is not in good standing, and the Board *"may
  suspend or revoke the charter."*
- **American Legion (Art. XI, Sec. 2):** a post refusing to pay per capita
  *"shall, upon order of the Department Executive Committee, surrender its
  charter for cancellation."*
- **Elks:** $100 fine plus possible probation for late **Annual Report** filing;
  no penalty found specific to per-capita non-remittance.

## Unverified

**Eagles entirely** — the Grand Aerie Constitution & Statutes is sold, not
posted; treat Eagles as unresearched. The "Golden Age Eagle pays per capita
only" claim is **secondary sourcing — do not build on it.** Elks GLS 14.300 /
14.310 never read in original (reconstructed from three converging
Grand-Lodge-issued documents). **Moose: whether a *conferred* 50-year life
member generates ongoing per capita, and who pays — genuinely absent from both
the General Laws and the Administrator's Manual, and the single most likely place
a Moose implementation goes wrong.** Moose per-capita amount and due date
(delegated to the Board, unpublished). American Legion PUFL annual funding
mechanism. VFW treatment where a post has no relief fund or an insufficient one.

## Three questions for a real lodge officer

The Eagles and Moose gaps will not close from public sources.

1. **To an Elks Secretary:** *"When you remit dues for a member who's sick or in
   distress, does your April 1 membership report still count that member for
   Grand Lodge per capita — and does the Lodge write the check for that member's
   $38, or does the member still get billed the per-capita line separately?"*
   This distinguishes pattern 1 from pattern 4 in one answer.
2. **To a Moose Administrator:** *"For a member who got life membership
   conferred at 50 years rather than purchasing it — does Moose International
   still bill the Lodge a per-capita amount each year? Does anything land in
   Account 2515 for him?"*
3. **To an Eagles Secretary:** *"Does the Aerie owe per-capita on Golden Age
   Eagles and non-beneficial life members, and where does that money come from?
   Can you read me what Section 71.11 says?"*

Plus one cross-cutting: *"Do you accrue the liability at waiver, or only when
the invoice arrives?"*
